question.text:
We use the dictionary:

\begin{aligned}
M & : \text{domain of men} \\
s & : \text{Sharon} \\
N(x) & : x \text{ is nice} \\
L(x,y) & : x \text{ loves } y
\end{aligned}

Which of the following formulas corresponds to the sentence:
All nice men love Sharon.

  1. $\exists x \in M[N(x) \wedge L(x, s)]$
  2. $\exists x \in M[N(x) \rightarrow L(x, s)]$
  3. $\forall x \in M[N(x) \wedge L(x, s)]$
  4. $\forall x \in M[N(x) \rightarrow L(x, s)]$
question.subject: Mathematical Logic

question.text:
Consider the following two logical equivalences that express 'logical laws':
- $ eg orall x \in D f \equiv \exists x \in D eg f$
- $ eg(f \leftrightarrow g) \equiv eg f \leftrightarrow eg g$

Which of these hold?

  1. both
  2. only the first
  3. only the second
  4. none
question.subject: Mathematical Logic

question.text:
Which of the following formulas does not express that there is exactly one element of $D$ that has property $P(x)$ ?

  1. $\exists x \in D \forall y \in D[P(y) \leftrightarrow y=x]$
  2. $\exists x \in D[P(x) \wedge \forall y \in D[y \neq x \rightarrow \neg P(y)]]$
  3. $\exists x \in D P(x) \wedge \forall x_1, x_2 \in D\left[P\left(x_1\right) \wedge P\left(x_2\right) \rightarrow x_1=x_2\right]$
  4. $\exists x \in D \forall y \in D[P(y) \rightarrow y=x]$
question.subject: Mathematical Logic

question.text:
Which of the following formulas does not express that there is at most one element of $D$ that has property $P(x)$ ?

  1. $ orall x_1, x_2 \in D\left[P\left(x_1 ight) \wedge P\left(x_2 ight) ightarrow x_1=x_2 ight]$
  2. $ orall x_1, x_2 \in D\left[x_1 eq x_2 ightarrow eg P\left(x_1 ight) \vee eg P\left(x_2 ight) ight]$
  3. $ eg \exists x_1, x_2 \in D\left[x_1 eq x_2 \wedge P\left(x_1 ight) \wedge P\left(x_2 ight) ight]$
  4. $ eg \exists x_1, x_2 \in D\left[P\left(x_1 ight) \wedge x_1 eq x_2 ightarrow eg P\left(x_2 ight) ight]$
